1002.title: The trains
1002.hook: in 1947 trains of refugees crossed the new border, and violence struck on both sides
1002.howItsDone: Sikh families with Partition memories retell them at home and in the gurdwara, and the Ardas said at the close of every service asks for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rawalpindi and the women of Thoa Khalsa, and your line was hold them gently. Did someone trust you with a hard story? Today the border is drawn, and people start to move. Day one thousand two.

A small railway station at night, beside a river, in a village where Sikhs and Muslims share the same fields and the same gossip. A train comes in from across the new border, and nobody gets off. That's a scene from Train to Pakistan, a novel by the Sikh writer Khushwant Singh, set in the summer of 1947. The train is fiction. The trains behind it were not. When the line between India and Pakistan was drawn, families who found themselves on the wrong side packed what they could carry and crowded onto trains going the other way.
screen: `A STATION AT NIGHT.` → `NOBODY GETS OFF.` → `THE TRAINS BEHIND THE NOVEL.`

segments.voice: First, both directions. Hindus and Sikhs traveled east into India. Muslims traveled west into Pakistan. The same rails carried frightened people both ways, with children on laps and bundles on the roof. Second, both sides of the line. Trains were attacked, and the killing was done by mobs on each side of the new border, to people on each side. Sikhs suffered terribly in 1947, and some Sikhs also did terrible things to Muslim neighbors. Honest histories of Partition say this plainly, and so does Khushwant Singh's novel. Third, the hero of the story. In the novel, men plan to stop a train of Muslims bound for Pakistan by stretching a rope across a bridge. A rough Sikh villager named Jugga, a man the police call a bad character, climbs up in the dark and cuts the rope, and is shot doing it. The train goes through. A novelist who lived through that year chose to end his book with a Sikh giving his life for a train full of Muslims. Fourth, the old words. At Ang 1299 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that since he found the company of the holy, he sees no one as an enemy and no one as a stranger, and he gets along with all. And every Ardas ends by asking for sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of our side. All. That's today's line: pray for every side.
screen: `TRAINS CARRIED PEOPLE BOTH WAYS.` · `VIOLENCE ON BOTH SIDES OF THE LINE.` · `JUGGA CUTS THE ROPE.` · `ANG 1299: NO ENEMY, NO STRANGER.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for every side. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the families on those trains: going east, going west, Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and the people on each platform waiting for someone who didn't come. Don't sort them. Hold them all at once. Breathe in, and widen the circle. Breathe out, and leave no one outside it. If you pray, you can ask for sarbat da bhala, the good of all, the way the Ardas does. If you don't, simply wish them all well. The bell holds the time.
The trains. The crowded trains of 1947 that carried refugees both ways across the new border, and were attacked on both sides. Today's word.
Your line: pray for every side. Today, when you hear about a conflict, wish well to the people on the side you don't usually think about. Day one thousand two.

1003.title: Nankana left behind
1003.hook: the new border left Guru Nanak's birthplace in Pakistan
1003.howItsDone: The Ardas said at the close of Sikh worship asks for open access to and care of the gurdwaras separated from the panth, and on special days groups of Sikh pilgrims travel to Nankana Sahib and other gurdwaras in Pakistan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trains, and Jugga cutting the rope on the bridge. Your line was pray for every side. Who did you wish well that you usually leave out? Today, a place that stayed on the far side. Day one thousand three.

Near the end of the Ardas, after the Gurus and the martyrs have been remembered, comes a request about places. It asks God to grant the Khalsa open access to, and care of, the gurdwaras and holy places that were separated from the panth. Those few words carry a whole map. When the border was drawn, the town where Guru Nanak was born, Nankana Sahib, fell on the Pakistan side. So did other places from his life. People who had walked there for festivals now looked west at a line they couldn't freely cross.
screen: `A REQUEST NEAR THE END OF THE ARDAS.` → `THE BIRTHPLACE ACROSS THE LINE.` → `LOOKING WEST.`

segments.voice: First, what was left. This path has already been to Nankana: the stories of Guru Nanak's birth and childhood, and earlier this year, the reformers who died to free its gurdwara. Now a border runs between that town and the Sikhs of Indian Punjab. The place didn't change. The way to it did. Second, the Ardas. The request for open access is said at the close of Sikh worship, in gurdwaras far from Punjab as well as in it. So the loss isn't kept in a museum. It's spoken, day after day, as a hope. Third, the pilgrims. On special days, groups of Sikh pilgrims are given permission to cross and visit Nankana Sahib and other gurdwaras in Pakistan, and the Sikhs who live there and the people of the town receive them. The way is narrow, but it isn't closed. Fourth, the longing. In a hymn at Ang 96 of the Guru Granth Sahib, which tradition says he wrote while far from his Guru, Guru Arjan writes that his mind longs for the Guru's sight like the rain-bird crying out for the drop of rain. The Sikh tradition already had words for missing a holy presence you can't reach. Those words fit a border too. And in the Gurus' hymns, the One is not kept on one side of any line. You can pray toward Nankana from anywhere. That's today's line: left behind. Not forgotten. Left behind, and asked for, and longed for.
screen: `THE PLACE DIDN'T CHANGE. THE WAY DID.` · `THE ARDAS ASKS FOR OPEN ACCESS.` · `PILGRIMS CROSS WHEN ALLOWED.` · `ANG 96: LIKE THE RAIN-BIRD.` · then, large: `LEFT BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes facing a place you can't visit. Sit, and if you know the direction, turn a little toward it: a grandparent's village, a house that was sold, a country you left, a grave far away, or Nankana itself. Close your eyes. Walk there in your mind: the road in, the door, the smell of the air. Breathe in, and arrive. Breathe out, and let the longing be there without fixing it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nankana left behind. Guru Nanak's birthplace, left on the Pakistan side of the new border, and remembered in the Ardas every day. Today's word.
Your line: left behind. Today, find one place you can't go back to, and say its name out loud once. Day one thousand three.

1004.title: Starting from nothing
1004.hook: refugee Sikhs rebuilt lives in Delhi and East Punjab
1004.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karo, earning by honest work, alongside naam japo and vand chhako, and Punjabi families descended from Partition refugees retell how their elders rebuilt their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana across the border, and your line was left behind. Did you say the name of a place you can't go back to? Today, the people who arrived with nothing. Day one thousand four.

What do you sell when everything you owned is on the other side of a border? A few combs, some bars of soap, a row of pencils, laid out on a wooden crate turned upside down on a Delhi pavement. Behind the crate, a man in a turban who, a few months earlier, owned land or a shop in a town that is now in Pakistan. Stories like this are told in Punjabi families: a grandfather who sold things off a crate, a grandmother who sewed through the night, a camp of tents, a first rented room. The refugees came into Delhi and East Punjab carrying what they could hold. Then they started again.
screen: `A CRATE ON A DELHI PAVEMENT.` → `COMBS, SOAP, PENCILS.` → `THEN THEY STARTED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the arrival. Families who had crossed the border lived in camps, in shelters, in the homes of relatives already crowded. Land, shops and houses were gone. Some had lost people too, and carried that along with the bundles. Second, the work. Sikh teaching sums up a life in three short instructions often traced to Guru Nanak: remember the Name, earn by honest work, and share what you have. Naam japo, kirat karo, vand chhako. The middle one is kirat, honest labor. In the stories families tell of those years, it was the thing they could still hold on to when nothing else was left. A crate became a stall, a stall a shop, a shop a living. Third, the Guru's measure. Early on this path you met Bhai Lalo, the carpenter of Saidpur. Tradition says Guru Nanak ate Lalo's coarse bread, earned by his own hands, and turned down a rich man's feast. Not the one who had the most. The one who worked honestly and shared. Fourth, the sharing. In the stories of those years, langar was cooked even in the camps: the free kitchen, now feeding people who had nothing, sometimes cooked by people who had very little more. Starting over and giving away turned out not to be opposites. That's today's line: from nothing. Not nothing at all. From nothing but hands, honest work, and a shared pot.
screen: `CAMPS, SHELTERS, CROWDED ROOMS.` · `KIRAT KARO: EARN BY HONEST WORK.` · `LALO'S BREAD: EARNED, AND SHARED.` · `LANGAR IN THE CAMPS.` · then, large: `FROM NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a beginning. Sit, and let your hands rest open. Think of one thing you've wanted to start and haven't, because you didn't feel ready: a skill, a garden, a savings jar, a letter, an apology. Don't plan the whole of it. Find only the very first step, small enough to do today with what you already have. Breathe in, and see your hands doing it. Breathe out, and let go of waiting for the perfect start. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Starting from nothing. The refugees of Partition rebuilding their lives in Delhi and East Punjab, with honest work and shared bread. Today's word.
Your line: from nothing. Today, take the first small step of that one thing, with what you already have. Day one thousand four.

1005.title: A poet's lament
1005.hook: Amrita Pritam wrote a lament for Punjab's daughters in 1947
1005.howItsDone: Amrita Pritam's poem to Waris Shah is read and sung by Punjabis remembering Partition, and the Guru Granth Sahib keeps the Punjabi verses of the Sufi Sheikh Farid alongside the Gurus' hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crate on a Delhi pavement, and your line was from nothing. Did you take the first small step? Today, someone who answered that year with a poem. Day one thousand five.

A young woman, a refugee herself, born into a Sikh family in a town that is now in Pakistan. Her name is Amrita Pritam. In 1947, with Punjab torn in two, she writes a poem. It doesn't call on a politician or a general. It calls on a poet who has been dead a very long time, a Muslim Sufi named Waris Shah, who wrote the old Punjabi love story of Heer and Ranjha. Her first line, in Punjabi, is a summons: today I call on Waris Shah. Why would a grieving Sikh woman call to a Muslim poet in his grave?
screen: `A REFUGEE, A SIKH FAMILY.` → `SHE WRITES A POEM.` → `TODAY I CALL ON WARIS SHAH.`

segments.voice: First, who she calls. Waris Shah wrote Heer, the long poem of a young woman of Punjab and her lover, and the sorrow that came to her. It's a story Punjabis of different faiths share. So Amrita Pritam goes to him as the poet who once wrote down the pain of one daughter of Punjab. Second, what she asks. In her poem, as she tells it, when one daughter of Punjab wept, Waris Shah wrote a whole tale of grief. Now the daughters of Punjab are weeping, and she asks him to speak from among the graves and turn the next page of his book of love. She speaks of poison mixed into the waters of Punjab, and of blood across its land. Third, what she doesn't do. The poem names no enemy. It doesn't ask for revenge, and it doesn't sort the dead into ours and theirs. The daughters in it are simply Punjab's daughters. It's a lament, a mourning song, and it holds the whole land at once. Fourth, an older bridge. Sikhs don't have to look outside their own scripture for a Muslim poet of Punjab. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps the Punjabi verses of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, alongside the hymns of the Gurus; you met his verses earlier in this block, at Nankana and at Jaito. A Sikh-born poet reaching across faiths to a Sufi was walking a road Punjab already knew. That's today's line: a poet mourned. In a year of knives, someone picked up a pen and grieved for everyone.
screen: `SHE CALLS ON WARIS SHAH.` · `ONE DAUGHTER THEN, THE DAUGHTERS NOW.` · `NO ENEMY NAMED, NO REVENGE.` · `FARID'S VERSES IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.` · then, large: `A POET MOURNED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of mourning without blame. Sit, and let the breath go slow. Bring to mind one sorrow in the world right now, near or far. Hold it the way the poem does: without naming an enemy, without choosing sides among the grieving. Breathe in, and let it be heavy. Breathe out, and let it be shared. Afterward, if you'd like, read about Amrita Pritam's poem, and about Waris Shah, and see what you hear in them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
A poet's lament. Amrita Pritam's poem of 1947, calling on Waris Shah to write the grief of Punjab's daughters. Today's word.
Your line: a poet mourned. Today, look up her poem and read about it, and notice that it names no enemy. Day one thousand five.

1006.title: Bhagat Puran Singh
1006.hook: a man who carried a disabled boy on his back for years founded the Pingalwara home in Amritsar
1006.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhagat Puran Singh as an example of seva, and the Pingalwara in Amritsar, the home he founded, still cares for disabled and destitute people, supported by volunteers and donors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amrita Pritam calling on Waris Shah, and your line was a poet mourned. Did you read about her poem? Today, someone who answered the same years with his back. Day one thousand six.

Nobody comes back for the boy. He is small, he cannot walk, and someone has left him at the gate of a gurdwara in Lahore. The man who finds him is a sevadar there, a volunteer who sweeps floors and carries water. His name is Puran Singh. He picks the boy up. Then, the story goes, he simply doesn't put him down. For years he carries the boy on his back wherever he goes: to the gurdwara, through the streets, to the library where he likes to read. When the border comes, the two of them cross it together, into a refugee camp in Amritsar.
screen: `NOBODY COMES BACK FOR HIM.` → `HE PICKS HIM UP.` → `HE DOESN'T PUT HIM DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the boy. People who tell the story give him the name Piara, beloved. He couldn't care for himself, and nobody else would. Puran Singh had no money, no home of his own and no organization. He had a back. Second, the carrying. This is the part people remember, and it's very plain. He fed the boy, washed him, and carried him, day after day, for years. No committee decided it. No one paid him. Third, the home. In Amritsar after Partition, Puran Singh began taking in others nobody wanted: the disabled, the abandoned, the dying, people left in the streets. Out of that grew the Pingalwara, a home for them, which still cares for people in Amritsar. People began calling him Bhagat, which means devotee. Nobody appointed him; people saw how he lived. Fourth, the root. Seva, selfless service, has run through this whole path. At Ang 26 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that it is by serving in this world that a person finds a place of honor in God's court. Puran Singh's life reads like that line acted out. Seva without a stage, without a sign on the door, with a boy's arms around his neck. That's today's line: he carried him. And the city that holds the Golden Temple's kitchen also holds the house he built.
screen: `A BOY NOBODY CAME BACK FOR.` · `CARRIED, DAY AFTER DAY.` · `PINGALWARA: A HOME FOR THE UNWANTED.` · `ANG 26: SERVE IN THIS WORLD.` · then, large: `HE CARRIED HIM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a load. Sit, and feel the weight of your own body on the chair or the floor. Notice your back: what it holds up, without being asked, all day. Now bring to mind one person near you who is carrying something heavy right now: an illness, a child, a debt, grief, a job that's too much. Breathe in, and feel their weight beside your own. Breathe out, and ask yourself which small corner of it you could lift today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhagat Puran Singh. The sevadar who carried a disabled boy on his back for years and founded the Pingalwara home in Amritsar. Today's word.
Your line: he carried him. Today, carry part of someone's load: a bag, a chore, an errand, an hour of listening. Day one thousand six.

1007.title: The Punjabi Suba campaign
1007.hook: years of peaceful campaigning for a Punjabi-language state
1007.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Punjabi Suba campaign as a peaceful political movement led by the Akali Dal; its morchas, with volunteers courting arrest, are told in histories of modern Punjab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat Puran Singh, and your line was he carried him. Whose load did you lift, even for a minute? Today the story moves from one man's back to a whole people's voice. Day one thousand seven.

A line of volunteers walks out of a gurdwara, singing, toward the police. They are not carrying weapons. They are carrying a slogan. The police arrest them, and the next day another line walks out, and the day after that another. The jails fill. The singing goes on. What they want sounds almost ordinary: a state where the language people speak at home, Punjabi, is the language of the schools, the courts and the government offices. The word for a state or province is suba. Today, the long campaign for a Punjabi Suba.
screen: `VOLUNTEERS WALK OUT SINGING.` → `THE JAILS FILL.` → `A STATE FOR A LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the ask. After independence, India began redrawing its states around the languages people spoke. Punjab was left as it was, a mix of Punjabi speakers and Hindi speakers. The Akali Dal, a Sikh political party, asked for a state shaped around Punjabi, written in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib. Second, the way it was asked. Leaders like Master Tara Singh and later Sant Fateh Singh led morchas, peaceful campaigns where volunteers marched, courted arrest and went to jail by choice. There were fasts, and promises to fast. It was the same method this path met earlier at Guru ka Bagh and the gurdwara reform: no striking back, and no going away. Third, the other side. Not everyone wanted it. Some in Delhi worried that a state drawn around Punjabi would really be a state drawn around religion. Some Punjabi Hindus said their language was Hindi, and the question of language got tangled up with the question of faith. The campaign was asking a hard question in a crowded room. Fourth, the root. In the Guru Granth Sahib, at Ang 661, Guru Nanak says that as long as we live in this world, we should listen a little and speak a little. A fair ask does both. It keeps speaking, and it keeps listening, even when the answer is no, and no again. That's today's line: ask, and ask again.
screen: `A STATE SHAPED AROUND PUNJABI.` · `MORCHAS: MARCH, COURT ARREST, FAST.` · `SOME FEARED A STATE OF ONE FAITH.` · `LISTEN A LITTLE, SPEAK A LITTLE.` · then, large: `ASK, AND ASK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to rehearse a fair ask. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing you've asked for and been refused: from a parent, a boss, a landlord, a friend. Breathe in, and say the ask to yourself plainly, in one sentence, with no blame in it. Breathe out, and hear their reason for saying no, as fairly as you can. Breathe in, ask again. Breathe out, listen again. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru between the two. The bell holds the time.
The Punjabi Suba campaign. The long, peaceful push for a state shaped around the Punjabi language, carried on through marches, arrests and fasts. Today's word.
Your line: ask, and ask again. Today, go back to one fair request you dropped, and make it once more, calmly, ready to listen to the answer. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: Punjab reorganised, 1966
1008.hook: Punjab is reorganised into a smaller Punjabi-speaking state
1008.howItsDone: Sikhs and other Punjabis remember the reorganization of Punjab as the end of the Punjabi Suba campaign; Punjabi in Gurmukhi is taught in Punjab's schools and used in its government.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Punjabi Suba campaign, and your line was ask, and ask again. Did you make one fair request a second time? Today the asking gets an answer, and a week ends. Day one thousand eight.

A map is redrawn, and overnight a village's address changes without a single house moving. That is what happened across Punjab in the year in today's title. One state was cut into parts. Lines were drawn through districts, and families woke up in a new state, or in the same state with a new shape. For the Sikhs who had marched and gone to jail for it, the answer had finally come: a Punjab where Punjabi was the language of the state. A smaller Punjab, and a home for a language.
screen: `THE MAP IS REDRAWN.` → `ONE STATE, CUT INTO PARTS.` → `A HOME FOR A LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: First, the new lines. The old Punjab was divided. The Punjabi-speaking areas became the new, smaller Punjab. Hindi-speaking areas became a new state, Haryana. Some hill districts were joined to Himachal Pradesh. Second, what it gave. Punjabi, written in Gurmukhi, became the language of the state: of its schools, its offices, its signboards. Gurmukhi is the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in, and tradition credits Guru Angad, the second Guru, with shaping it for the Sikhs. So the letters a child learned at school were the letters of the Guru's word. Third, what it left open. The new city of Chandigarh was not simply handed to Punjab; it became a shared capital for Punjab and Haryana. Questions about river waters and borders stayed unsettled, and they come back in the days ahead. Some Sikhs felt they had won the language and lost some of what they had asked for alongside it. Fourth, a look back. This week began on the trains of Partition. Then came Nankana Sahib, left behind across a new border; families starting from nothing; a poet mourning Punjab's daughters; Bhagat Puran Singh carrying a boy on his back; and the long campaign of asking. A week that started with a border cutting Punjab apart ends with a border drawn on purpose, around a language. That's today's line: the language home.
screen: `ONE PUNJAB, DIVIDED.` · `PUNJABI IN GURMUKHI, THE STATE'S LANGUAGE.` · `CHANDIGARH AND THE RIVERS LEFT OPEN.` · `FROM PARTITION TO A LANGUAGE HOME.` · then, large: `THE LANGUAGE HOME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your first language. Sit comfortably, and let the breath come and go. Whatever language you first heard as a child, bring it back now. Silently, say one word from it: the word for mother, or home, or water, or bread. Breathe in with that word. Breathe out, and notice who said it to you first. If English is your first language, find the oldest word you remember from a grandparent's mouth. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Punjab reorganised. The old state redrawn into a smaller Punjab where Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, became the language of the state, with Haryana and Himachal taking the rest. Today's word.
Your line: the language home. Today, speak or write a few words in your first language, or the language of someone you love, and let it sound like home. Day one thousand eight.
